newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Compaq says direct sale model inefficient.
newsitem.headline: Compaq says direct sale model inefficient.

text.p: The direct sales approach by its rivals Dell Computer Corp and Gateway 2000 Inc is inefficient, a senior official from Compaq Computer Corp said on Friday.
"We see inefficiencies in direct models," Greg Petsch, Compaq's senior vice president of corporate operations and quality said after delivering a speech.
He said the system is unable to cope with larger customers from the corporate side.

Companies like Dell and Gateway, which sell directly to customers without going through distributors and other indirect channels, was "well designed for small quantities" like to small and medium-sized companies, Petsch said.
"But as they move into corporate accounts, it is not so efficient," he said.
Petsch said the indirect channels were still needed to provide the service and support, for instance, like testing systems on site for corporate customers, which the direct model did not offer.
Dell and Gateway have said they managed to sell their systems at lower price by cutting out the middlemen.
Dell's chairman Michael Dell last month said he was confused by how Compaq's move to sell custom-made computers, both through resellers and directly to customers, could lower prices.
Petsch on Friday told a Singapore audience about Compaq's process of "re-engineering" and how it had moved to a "hybrid" system.
This "hybrid" system combines customizing products to customers' requirements and cutting down inventories, resulting in lower costs and faster delivery.
Petsch said Compaq was aiming to meet its US$40 billion sales target by 2000 with the same number of plants it has now.

By then, Compaq would have almost no warehousing as it would customize products directly in its plants and ship them directly to customers. Their distributors would act as agents and service and support providers.
It also saw more and more customers being able to order through online systems, which would further reduce costs.
Compaq currently has five plants, including one in Singapore. It has set up a "configuration centre" in Australia where products are sent for final design as customers require.
Compaq is looking at eventually doing all configurations at its plants.

Petsch said Compaq's Singapore facility played an important role in its move to customisation. It is in the process of setting up an Asian Consumer Development Centre that should be able to deliver specific customer software and literature.

The Singapore plant produces desktops and consumer systems for the Asia Pacific region, and designs and distributes portables for the global market. Singapore is starting to produce enterprise systems for businesses as well.

Petsch added that Singapore now produced 58 percent of Compaq's printed circuit boards, and production would rise further as more surface mount technology (SMT) lines were added in the next couple of years.
